name: Eipo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Heeschen, Volker. 1978. The Mek languages of Irian Jaya with special reference to the Eipo language [sect. 2 'Sketch of Eipo grammar', pp. 21-41; 2.1 'Sound system and alphabet', pp. 21-23]. Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya Development VII(2): 3-46. Jayapura: Lembaga Antropologi, Universitas Cenderawasih / SIL. Supporting: Heeschen, Volker. 1992. The position of the Mek languages of Irian Jaya among the Papuan languages. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 148(3/4): 465-488, p. 470.
catalog_locator: p. 23 (sect. 2.1, last two paragraphs before '2.2 Morphology'; PDF spread page 13, right-hand page, crops). Supporting: p. 22 (main stress of a word conditions /e/), p. 29 (compounds under one main stress), Heeschen 1992: 470.
catalog_quote: Stress occurs in two syllable words (1) on that syllable which has more satellites, cp. bikle ['bɩklə] 'he knows' and biisiik [bi'sik] 'way, direction'; (2) it does not occur word finally in open syllables after consonant clusters, cp. bilyam [bɩ'l̡am] 'you shall go' and bilye ['bɩl̡ə] 'going'. Where these criteria do not work, e.g. in binmal 'he is going', the placing of the stress depends on the intonation patterns of the utterance. Words of more than two syllables can be traced back to the two basic rules. In most cases stress cooccurs with a high rising tone. But for a small subset of the nouns, all of which are deverbal derivations, this rule does not apply, cp. fokna ['fɔkna] 'sexual intercourse' and fokná ['fɔ̀kná] or ['fɔ̀knáʔ] 'whistling', where stress and tone are dissociated. Instead of writing or indicating the glottal stop, which seems to be at the origin of this high rising tone, words like fokná shall be marked by /´/, because the same symbol can be used in all other cases where the indication of stress (occurring with high rising tone) seems to be appropriate.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Rendered spread page 13 afresh at 110 dpi and read the right-hand page, headed "23.", myself ( eipo1242_check/), and compared with the compiler the page scan, and the scanned the page scan. The quoted paragraph is on that page, verbatim in its prose: "Stress occurs in two syllable words (1) on that syllable which has more satellites, cp. bikle [..] 'he knows' and biisiik [bi'sik] 'way, direction'; (2) it does not occur word finally in open syllables after consonant clusters,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed position. In a disyllable the stress goes to the syllable with more consonantal 'satellites' (the more complex/heavier syllable: bík.le but bii.síik), with the restriction that a word-final open syllable following a consonant cluster is never stressed (bil.yám but bíl.ye). When neither criterion decides (e.g. binmal 'he is going') placement follows the intonation of the utterance. Longer words are said to follow the same two rules. Stress normally coincides with a high rising tone. Heeschen 1992: 470 adds that in Eipomek and the dialects to its east 'accent is phonemic'. (Phonetic brackets in the quote approximate the typescript's IPA: bikle ['bɪklə], bilyam [bɪ'lʲam], bilye ['bɪlʲə]; see page crop.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. Compounds: 'Serialization of two or more nouns joined under one main stress, e.g. mek katum "bank"' (sect. 2.2.2, p. 29, scanned).
new_statements.exceptions: A small subset of nouns, all deverbal derivations with a (historical) final glottal stop, dissociate stress and tone: fokna ['fɔkna] 'sexual intercourse' vs fokná ['fɔ̀kná] ~ ['fɔ̀knáʔ] 'whistling' (p. 23; also p. 12 as a minimal pair). Cases like binmal where the two criteria do not apply are decided by utterance intonation. p. 12 says stress 'seems to be partially phonemic in the east' (Ok Bab), i.e. eastern Mek, not Eipo itself.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for disyllables (the bulk of the vocabulary); for undetermined words the domain is effectively the utterance (intonation). Noun compounds bear one main stress. The sketch is a 1978 typescript-era first description (author says the phonology is tentative); the 1998 reference grammar, which could not be opened, presumably supersedes it.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1978 sketch describes the Eipo of the Eipomek valley proper (Heeschen's item (1): 'Eipo, language of Eipomek, lik yure', data collected at 140°E 4°28'S), i.e. Eipomek [eipo1242] itself, western Mek; Heeschen notes Larye (Una, unaa1239) and Tani are also spoken in Eipomek. The 1992 'accent is phonemic' remark covers 'Eipomek and the dialects east of Eipomek'. The 1978 p. 12 remark on partially phonemic stress concerns Ok Bab (Ketengban, eastern Mek), not Eipo.

tone_statements.citation: Heeschen, Volker. 1978. The Mek languages of Irian Jaya with special reference to the Eipo language [sect. 2 'Sketch of Eipo grammar', 2.1 Phonology]. Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya Development VII(2): 3-41. Jayapura: Lembaga Antropologi, Universitas Cenderawasih / SIL.
tone_statements.quote: High rising tone is conditioned by the presence or loss of word final glottal stop. In Eipo we find minimal pairs of the following kind: fokná 'whistling', fokna 'sexual intercourse', phonetically ['fɔknáˀ] and ['fɔkna]. … Thus tonal features develop only in certain restricted environments … tones have to be marked only on a very limited set of the vocabulary. … In most cases stress cooccurs with a high rising tone. But for a small subset of the nouns, all of which are deverbal derivations, this rule does not apply … where stress and tone are dissociated.

tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Marginal tone: a high rising tone normally goes with the stressed syllable but contrasts on a few deverbal nouns (fokná 'whistling' vs fokna), derived from a final glottal stop; weight-based stress.

tone.quote: Die Schreibung il „er, sie, es” statt Wb. el ist konstant, möglicherweise beeinflusst durch die tonlose, akzentlose Stellung in häufig zu hörenden Nominalphrasen, z.B. ilin [ɪlin], [əlin] „sein oder ihr Vater”. … für talebranmarurak und yanganmalye (zu d [d] und r [ɾ] s. Heeschen 1998: 120, zu den suprasegmentalen Eigenschaften Heeschen 1998: 131-136).
tone.translation: The spelling il 'he, she, it' instead of (dictionary) el is constant, possibly influenced by the toneless, accentless position in frequently heard noun phrases, e.g. ilin [ɪlin], [əlin] 'his or her father'. … for talebranmarurak and yanganmalye (on d [d] and r [ɾ] see Heeschen 1998: 120, on the suprasegmental properties Heeschen 1998: 131-136).
